bonus_mechanics: New Mexico personal income tax starts from federal adjusted gross income (TRD: 'Personal income tax in New Mexico starts with the Federally Adjusted Gross Income (FAGI) from your federal return'). The 2021 PIT-ADJ lists the only permitted additions (lines 1-4: tax-exempt bond interest, federal NOL carryover, 529 refunds, conservation-land charitable deduction) and says 'If an item is not listed, it is not a valid New Mexico addition, exemption, or deduction for this schedule.' There is no depreciation or 168(k) line, so the federal bonus deduction flows through Schedule C/E/F into FAGI unchanged.
special_rules: No NM basis difference arises for a sole proprietor or rental owner, so one depreciation schedule serves federal and NM. NM is a community property state (relevant to splitting business income between spouses). A NM NOL is limited to a federal NOL, no carryback, 19-year carryforward for losses incurred on or after 1 Jan 2013 (PIT-ADJ line 7). Gross receipts tax is a separate transaction tax with no depreciation computation (not researched).
source_citation: NM TRD, 2021 PIT-ADJ Instructions (General Information; lines 1-4 additions; no depreciation line); TRD Personal Income Tax Overview https://www.tax.newmexico.gov/individuals/personal-income-tax-information-overview/; NMSA 7-2-2 ('adjusted gross income' = IRC 62 'as that section may be amended or renumbered')
verify_note: PIT-ADJ text read in full 2026-10-06. The 'rolling' label rests on a search-result excerpt of NMSA 7-2-2 (statute pages on nmlegis.gov and Justia returned HTTP 403, so the statute was not read). Federal 179 and 100% bonus figures are the federal amounts, not stated by NM. The PIT-1 instructions were not read.

bonus_mechanics: NY does not allow the federal 168(k) special depreciation for property placed in service on or after 1 Jun 2003 (tax years beginning after 31 Dec 2002). Add back ALL federal depreciation deducted on 168(k) property (IT-225 addition A-209, from IT-398 col G) and subtract NY depreciation computed 'under IRC section 167, as that section would have applied to the property if it had been acquired on September 10, 2001' i.e. ordinary MACRS with no special allowance (IT-225 subtraction S-213, IT-398 col F). Year of disposition: S-214 = total federal depreciation minus total NY depreciation on that property. Exceptions: qualified resurgence zone property and NY Liberty Zone property (IRC 1400L(b)(2)). Read on the 2025 IT-398 and the 2022-2024 IT-225-I; the 2021 forms were not read.
change_note: For taxable years beginning before 1 Jan 2022 Tax Law 607(a) provides that 'any amendments made to the internal revenue code of nineteen hundred eighty-six after March first, two thousand twenty shall not apply to this article'.
special_rules: Qualified improvement property (QIP): NY personal income tax does NOT conform to the CARES Act QIP changes (15-year MACRS, 20-year ADS) for tax years before 2022 (TAX FAQ 'New York State tax implications of federal COVID relief for tax years beginning before January 1, 2022'); QIP therefore keeps its pre-CARES class life (39-year) for NY, differences reported on IT-558 for 2020-2021 per the FAQ. 179: no NY modification found, so the federal 179 limit applies (the 1,050,000 / 2,620,000 figure is the Rev. Proc. 2020-45 inflation adjustment, not a post-3/1/2020 amendment). The A-209/S-213 adjustments are made on the full amounts even if passive-activity limits cut the federal deduction (Tax Law 612(b)(8), (c)(16), per IT-398). Resident and part-year/nonresident filers complete IT-398 as a full-year resident.
source_citation: NY Tax Law 607(a) (nysenate.gov); Tax Law 612(b)(8), (c)(16) as cited in IT-398 instructions; NY TAX 'New York State tax implications of federal COVID relief for tax years beginning before January 1, 2022' https://www.tax.ny.gov/pit/cares-act-faq.htm; 2025 IT-398 https://www.tax.ny.gov/pdf/current_forms/it/it398_fill_in.pdf
verify_note: Statute and FAQ read via the fetch summariser (607(a) text returned verbatim and confirmed on a second fetch). The 2021 IT-225-I / IT-398 were not read; the 168(k) rule is taken from the 2025 IT-398 ('For tax years beginning after December 31, 2002') and the 2022-2024 IT-225-I. 179 conformity is inferred from the absence of any 179 modification in the instructions read, not from a sentence.

special_rules: The CARES Act QIP changes apply from tax years beginning on or after 1 Jan 2022 under the rolling rule; how NY treats QIP placed in service 2018-2021 and depreciated at 39 years for NY (catch-up or not) was not found. 179: no NY modification found; federal limit applies. Passive-activity rule as 2021.

bonus_mechanics: 2025 IT-398 (read in full): 'For tax years beginning after December 31, 2002, NYS does not allow the federal special depreciation deduction for IRC § 168(k) property ... placed in service inside or outside NYS after May 31, 2003. Instead, you are allowed a NYS depreciation deduction determined under IRC § 167, as that section would have applied to the property if it had been acquired on September 10, 2001.' Addition A-209 = federal depreciation deducted on the property (IT-398 col G); subtraction S-213 = NY depreciation (col F), computed with the convention from federal Form 4562 col E and any consistent method allowed 'without regard to § 168(k)'; basis is reduced by any 179 expensing; disposition S-214. So the new 100% bonus for property acquired after 19 Jan 2025 (and the 40% on earlier-acquired property) is disallowed. Layer check: Rev. Proc. 2024-40 (40%; 179 at 1,250,000 / 3,130,000) is superseded by P.L. 119-21, but NY disregards bonus either way; for 179 NY has no figure of its own.
change_note: Notice N-26-1 (16 Jun 2026), under the 2026-2027 NY budget: NY does not conform to IRC 168(n) accelerated depreciation for qualified production property or to the OBBBA domestic R&E expensing (IRC 174/174A), for tax years beginning on or after 1 Jan 2025. 168(n): add back the full federal deduction (A-209) and subtract depreciation 'calculated as if the special depreciation election had not been made' (S-213). R&E: add back in full (A-225), subtract by amortizing over 60 months (S-221 for expenses on/after 1 Jan 2025; S-222 for earlier). Penalty and interest relief is available for timely filed or amended returns reporting these modifications. The notice does not mention 168(k) or 179.
special_rules: New 2025 modification A-223: an institutional real estate investor (10 or more residential properties of no more than two dwelling units in NYS, fiduciary managing pooled funds, 30,000,000 or more assets under management) must add back federal depreciation on those covered properties and NYS allows no depreciation on them; IT-398 must not be used for them (Tax Law 208.9(c-4); start year not confirmed). Passive-activity rule as 2021. NYC resident personal income tax follows the state base (NY TAX FAQ); NYC unincorporated business tax not researched. 179 for 2025: no NY modification found; the OBBBA 2,500,000 / 4,000,000 limit flows through under the rolling rule (inference).
source_citation: NY 2025 Form IT-398 General instructions; 2025 Form IT-225-I (A-209, A-223, S-213, S-214; no mention of P.L. 119-21); Notice N-26-1 https://www.tax.ny.gov/forms/n-notices/n-26-1.htm; Tax Law 607(a), 612(b)

bonus_mechanics: NC decouples from 168(k) and 168(n) bonus. 2021 D-401 Schedule S line 3: 'North Carolina did not adopt the 100% bonus depreciation provisions in IRC sections 168(k) or 168(n) for property placed in service for tax year 2021. You must add 85% of the amount of bonus depreciation deducted on your federal return to your state return.' Then 'you may deduct 20% of the amount added back in the first five taxable years beginning with tax year 2022' (Schedule S line 22 for 2016-2020 add-backs, lines 22f/23f). Net: 15% of the federal bonus is effectively allowed in year 1; the other 85% comes back in five equal 17% (= 20% x 85%) slices over 2022-2026. Regular MACRS on the whole basis continues; the add-back is an AGI adjustment on Schedule S, not a separate depreciation schedule.
special_rules: Section 179 (Schedule S line 4): NC did not conform to the increased federal expense deduction or investment limits; NC dollar limit $25,000 and investment limit $200,000. Add back 85% of (federal 179 deduction minus the 179 deduction using NC limits); deduct 20% of that add-back in each of the five years beginning 2022 (line 23). Bonus asset basis (line 21, G.S. 105-153.6(e),(f)): on an actual or deemed transfer after 1 Jan 2013 with carryover federal basis, the transferee adds any remaining bonus deductions allowed to the asset's basis and depreciates the adjusted basis over the remaining life; the transferor gets no future deductions. Line 6/27 handle federal-vs-state basis differences on property disposed of. IRC reference as of 1 Apr 2021 (not tracking later federal changes). NC rate 5.25%. Pass-through owners: not researched whether the add-back is reported by the entity or the owner.
source_citation: NCDOR 2021 Form D-401 instruction booklet, Instructions for D-400 Schedule S (p.17 IRC date, lines 3, 4; p.19 lines 21-23); G.S. 105-153.6 as cited there; https://www.ncdor.gov/taxes-forms/individual-income-tax/filing-topics/adjustment-bonus-depreciation

bonus_mechanics: Add back 85% of the federal bonus deduction under 168(k) or 168(n) (Schedule S line 3), then deduct 20% of that add-back in each of the five years 2026-2030. 2025 Schedule S: 'North Carolina did not adopt the bonus depreciation provisions in IRC sections 168(k) or 168(n) for property placed in service for tax year 2025. You must add 85% of the amount of bonus depreciation deducted on your federal return'; 'you may deduct 20% of the amount added back in the first five taxable years beginning with tax year 2026'. This applies to the new 100% bonus on property acquired after 19 Jan 2025 and the 40% on earlier-acquired property, and to the new 168(n) qualified production property allowance, equally. Layer check: P.L. 119-21 changes the federal amount that is added back, not the 85% / 20% x 5 rule.
change_note: Session Law 2026-31 (SB 595, signed 2 Jul 2026) updated the IRC reference from 1 Jan 2023 to 5 Jul 2025, covering the OBBBA (NCDOR FAQ of 11 Sep 2026, Q2, Q11, Q12). The 2025 booklet (published before the Act) still says 1 Jan 2023 and states OBBBA changes 'DO NOT apply'; that sentence is superseded for 2025 returns. NCDOR FAQ Q44: 'Has the NC decoupling adjustment for bonus depreciation changed? No.' The same law adds an R&E decoupling (add back 80% of 174A(a) amounts, deduct 25% in each of the next four years; Schedule S line 15 and line 40) and does not allow the OBBBA tips, overtime, car-loan and senior deductions (taken after AGI). Returns filed before the Act may need amending.
special_rules: 179: NC limits stay $25,000 dollar / $200,000 investment (2025 booklet line 4); add back 85% of (federal 179 minus 179 at NC limits), deduct 20% a year for five years from 2026. Therefore the OBBBA 2,500,000 / 4,000,000 federal 179 limits (and Rev. Proc. 2024-40's 1,250,000 / 3,130,000) do not apply for NC. The 2025 booklet's 179 sentence predates SL 2026-31; the FAQ read does not mention 179. Line 23 for 2025 deducts 20% of the 2020-2024 bonus add-backs; line 24 the same for 179. Bonus asset basis rule (line 22). NC itemized: after the Act the real-estate-tax deduction follows the post-OBBBA IRC 164 cap but the mortgage-interest-plus-property-tax total stays capped at $20,000 (FAQ Q16). NC rate 4.25%, standard deduction unchanged (FAQ Q15).

bonus_mechanics: ND individual tax starts from federal taxable income: N.D.C.C. 57-38-30.3(2) defines North Dakota taxable income as 'the federal taxable income of an individual, estate, or trust as computed under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended, adjusted as follows' (subdivisions a-t: US interest, capital-gain/dividend exclusion, lump-sum, military pay, etc.). No subdivision adjusts depreciation, 168(k), 168(n) or 179, and 57-38-30.3(1) limits a taxpayer to 'those adjustments or credits that are specifically provided for in this section'. The 2021 Schedule ND-1SA (read) lists only renaissance zone, new or expanding business, organ donor, workforce recruitment, stillborn child, National Guard/Reserve pay and college reimbursement subtractions - no depreciation line. So federal bonus (100% for 2021) and 179 flow through.
special_rules: No state depreciation schedule: use the federal Form 4562 and Schedule C/E/F figures. ND starts from federal TAXABLE income (after the federal standard/itemized deduction), so there is no separate ND deduction add-back for depreciation. Sole proprietors may claim the new or expanding business income exemption (N.D.C.C. ch. 40-57.1; ND-1SA line for 2021: line 2) and renaissance zone exemption (line 1) against business income. A filer with no federal return computes a pro forma federal taxable income first (57-38-30.3(1)). N.D.C.C. 57-38-01(5)(a)-(c) retain 1983-1989 ACRS and section 168(f)(8) leasing nonadoption rules that matter only to pre-1990 property.
source_citation: N.D.C.C. 57-38-30.3(1), (2); 57-38-01(5), (13); 57-38-01.1 (federal taxable income as starting point); ND Office of State Tax Commissioner, 2021 Schedule ND-1SA (SFN 28710, 12-2021) https://www.tax.nd.gov/sites/www/files/documents/forms/individual/2021-iit/schedule-nd-1sa-2021.pdf; Individual Income Tax History https://www.tax.nd.gov/individual-income-tax-history ('perpetually federalized for tax years beginning after December 31, 1988')

'Follows federal' is established by an exhaustive adjustment list plus the form, not by a sentence naming bonus depreciation. 179 limit and bonus rate are the federal values.

Federal 100% bonus and the federal 179 limit flow through.

bonus_mechanics: Ohio decouples from 168(k) and 179 expensing by an add-back and a five-year give-back. R.C. 5747.01(A)(17) (current text via FindLaw, 'current as of January 01, 2026'): add 5/6 of the depreciation allowed by IRC 168(k), plus 5/6 of qualifying 179 expense; (A)(18): deduct one-fifth of the amount so added in each of the five succeeding taxable years. Substitutions: for taxable years beginning in 2012 or later, 2/3 replaces 5/6 (and 1/2 over two years is deducted) if the taxpayer's Ohio income tax withheld rose 10% or more over the prior year, and no add-back if the withholding increase equals or exceeds the depreciation; 'the entire' amount (6/6, deducted 1/6 over six years) replaces 5/6 if a net operating loss results from the depreciation. Default result: year 1 deduction keeps 1/6 (16.67%) of the federal 168(k) amount, the other 5/6 returns at 1/6 (= 1/5 x 5/6) of the add-back per year for five years. The agency FAQ (search excerpt, tax.ohio.gov Income - Bonus Depreciation): the amount subject to add-back is 'total 179 expense less $25,000 plus all 168(k) depreciation expense'. Reported on the Ohio Schedule A (the Schedule of Adjustments); the 2021 form was not read.
change_note: Ohio is a static-conformity state (R.C. 5701.11) updated by annual bills; tax.ohio.gov conformity table (via search excerpt): tax year 2021 prior effective date 31 Mar 2021, conformity date 17 Feb 2022, and the taxpayer may irrevocably elect either the IRC as of the close of the taxable year or the version to which Ohio conforms. The 168(k)/179 add-back sits outside the conformity election.
special_rules: The 179 add-back is limited to 179 expense above 'the amount that would have been allowed under section 179 as it existed on Dec. 31, 2002' (2025 booklet p.20); the agency FAQ excerpt calls this $25,000. The 200,000 phase-out figure is the investment threshold of the 2002 federal text and is NOT stated by Ohio, so treat it as unconfirmed. Deduction of prior-year add-backs is taken in equal increments in consecutive years, any unused portion is not carried forward, it may be taken after disposing of the asset, and it is NOT allowed in a year with a federal NOL, NOL carryback or NOL carryforward (carried to the next year without one). No add-back for 168(k)/179 depreciation passed through from a pass-through entity (PTE) in which the taxpayer owns less than 5% (2025 booklet p.20, applied here as a continuing statute rule). These adjustments are not 'business income' (not on the Schedule of Business Income). Pass-through and fiduciary filers (IT 4708, IT 4738, IT 1041, IT 1140) make their own add-back and report it on the IT K-1. Nonresident and part-year filers apportion the depreciation adjustment by business through the IT NRC (property 20%, payroll 20%, sales 60%). Ohio has no state NOL carryback of its own but follows the federal carryback years, limited by the add-back. Commercial Activity Tax (CAT) is a gross receipts tax with no depreciation computation (not researched).

bonus_mechanics: 2025 IT 1040 instructions (read in full, tax year 2025, printed as accurate to 27 Nov 2025), Schedule of Adjustments line 9 'IRC 168(k) and 179 Depreciation' (p.20): 'Add 5/6 of your bonus depreciation allowed under Internal Revenue Code section 168(k). Also add 5/6 of your depreciation expense allowed under Internal Revenue Code section 179 less the amount that would have been allowed under section 179 as it existed on Dec. 31, 2002. Replace 5/6 with 2/3 for employers who increased their Ohio income taxes withheld by at least 10% over the previous year. Replace 5/6 with 6/6 for taxpayers who incur a net operating loss for federal income tax purposes if the loss was a result of the 168(k) and/or 179 depreciation expenses.' No add-back for an employer whose Ohio withholding rose by at least its total 168(k) and 179 expense, or for pass-through depreciation where the taxpayer owns less than 5%. Line 27 'Deduction of prior year 168(k) and 179 depreciation add-backs' (p.22-23): 1/5 of prior-year 5/6 add-backs, 1/2 of 2/3 add-backs, 1/6 of 6/6 add-backs, in equal increments in consecutive years. The add-back applies to the federal 168(k) amount whatever the rate, so the new 100% bonus (property acquired after 19 Jan 2025) and the 40% on earlier-acquired property are both added back at 5/6. Layer check: Rev. Proc. 2024-40 (40%; 179 at 1,250,000 / 3,130,000) is superseded by P.L. 119-21 (100%; 2,500,000 / 4,000,000) for the federal amount, but Ohio's 5/6 rule and the 2002 179 baseline are unchanged by either.
change_note: Senate Bill 9 (136th General Assembly), signed 5 Mar 2026 with immediate effect, updates R.C. 5701.11 to 5 Mar 2026 and incorporates IRC changes after 7 Mar 2025, including P.L. 119-21 (OBBBA) (EY Tax News 9 Mar 2026 and OSCPA excerpts, secondary). A taxpayer with a tax year ending after 7 Mar 2025 and before 5 Mar 2026 may irrevocably elect, on the 2025 return, to use all IRC provisions effective in that year; without the election the IRC as of 7 Mar 2025 applies, which predates P.L. 119-21 (4 Jul 2025). The 2025 booklet (printed 27 Nov 2025) predates SB 9, and its line 11 'Federal conformity additions' / line 31 'Federal conformity deductions' (and the page tax.ohio.gov/conformity) carry the election adjustments. Ohio is reported to follow 168(n) (no add-back, because R.C. 5747.01(A)(17) names only 168(k) and 179) while keeping the 168(k) and 179 add-back; also reported to follow 174A and the 163(j) change (secondary).
special_rules: Business income: first $250,000 ($125,000 if married filing separately) of business income in federal AGI is deductible and the remainder is taxed at a flat 3% (2025 booklet p.11, 26-27). Per the 2025 booklet example, federal bonus depreciation reduces the Schedule E business income that goes on the Schedule of Business Income, while the line 9 add-back is a nonbusiness adjustment (agency FAQ excerpt: it is not business income). Nonbusiness rates for 2025: 0% to 26,050, 2.75% to 100,000, 3.125% above (p.18). NOL years: the line 27 deduction is suspended and carried forward (p.23, p.63); Schedule IT NOL line 3 uses the entire 168(k)/179 add-back for a carryback. 179 add-back is of the excess over the amount allowed under 179 as it existed on 31 Dec 2002; the FAQ excerpt says 25,000; the 200,000 phase-out is a 2002 federal figure and not stated by Ohio. Pass-through and fiduciary filers make their own add-back (IT 4708, IT 4738, IT 1041, IT 1140). Nonresidents apportion the adjustment per business (IT NRC Sections II-III: property 20%, payroll 20%, sales 60%). Guaranteed payments and wages from a pass-through entity in which the taxpayer owns 20% or more are reclassified as business income.
